messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Stochastic Volatility Models
parts:
On 3/28/13 1:25 PM, Carlos wrote:

> I am wondering how STAN deals with a non-linear model like a Stochastic Volatility (SV) one.

The same way it deals with all models -- converts the
model to a log probabilty function with gradients then
runs NUTS (or a simpler HMC) sampler. :-)

Matt Hoffman used some simple stochastic volatility models
to test NUTS vs. HMC in the paper (which is about to
be published in JMLR): http://arxiv.org/abs/1111.4246

> I attach here a stan file
> that describes an AR(2) process with SV (and other exogenous regressors), where the error term of the regression is
> parametrized as in Kim, Sephard and Chib (1998), that is,
>
> |
> exp(h(t)/2)*e(t),e(t)~N(0,1)
> |

Stan, like BUGS and JAGS, was designed to allow you to evaluate
different models. So you could try the Kim et al. parameterization.
Though I couldn't quite parse the left side of your statement
because I was expecting a scalar output but you seem to have
a pair.

Reparameterizations can help with sampling speed in Stan,
especially if the prior scale (size of variance) or
geometry (shape of covariance) can be controlled. There's
a chapter of the manual providing examples.

> The code compiles, and runs. However, I do not know if I am taking a too naive approach here and if the results that I
> am getting are not proper...

I'd start with some models for which you know what the
answer is, either because you simulated the data or you
have some other software that gave you the answer. Then you
can be confident it's working and go on from there (though
continuing to check with simulated data's always a good practice).

> SV models are tricky, and usually people (including myself) focus on the approximations
> derived in Kim et al's paper, or, more recently, using particle filters. Is there any reason why it should not work in
> STAN? If it works, I think this is a great improvement...

Nope, no reason at all --- it's the kind of example for which
we built Stan.

There are lots of things you can do to speed this model up with
vectorization.

This looks wrong:

for (n in 1:N)
H1noise ~ normal(0, ETAs);

You're sampling the same variable, H1noise, repeatedly. Given that
it's a vector, you probably just want to drop the for wrapper.

For the truncation case:

ar2 ~ normal(0,100) T[-1,1];

you don't need the truncation bounds because the parameters (0, 100)
and truncation bounds [-1,1] are both constant and Stan only needs
the (log) probabilty up to a constant term. You defined the constraints
on ar2 properly and that's all you need. Same thing with PHIH.

The are other easy wins for vectorization; you can write this

for (n in 1:N1){

MU1[n] ~ normal(0,100);
}

as

MU1 ~ normal(0,100);

- Bob

Sorry, I should have written the whole model...now that I see it again, it is not clear at all. In any case, it is just a state-space model, where the variance of the measurement equation changes over time, and follows a log normal distribution. For example, if we have an AR(1) process in the measurement equation,

Y(t)= alpha*Y(t-1) + exp(h(t)/2)*e(t)

 where e(t) is just white noise. The state equation for the volatilities,

h(t) = muh + phih*(h(t-1) - muh) +eta(t)
eta(t)~N(0,sigma)

and this is really the object of interest...

I'd start with some models for which you know what the 
answer is, either because you simulated the data or you 
have some other software that gave you the answer.  Then you 
can be confident it's working and go on from there (though 
continuing to check with simulated data's always a good practice).

I have just simulated data, with different parametrisations, and IT WORKS LIKE CHARM! 10,000 iterations in 15 seconds, and with great convergence properties. Infinitely better/faster than my MATLAB codes. Of course, the results for the extracted states are dependent on the signal-noise ratio, but that is a standard problem. With enough variation, STAN is great.

This looks wrong: 

     for (n in 1:N) 
       H1noise ~ normal(0, ETAs); 

You're sampling the same variable, H1noise, repeatedly.   Given that 
it's a vector, you probably just want to drop the for wrapper. 

For the truncation case: 

     ar2 ~ normal(0,100) T[-1,1]; 

you don't need the truncation bounds because the parameters (0, 100) 
and truncation bounds [-1,1] are both constant and Stan only needs 
the (log) probabilty up to a constant term.  You defined the constraints 
on ar2 properly and that's all you need.  Same thing with PHIH. 

The are other easy wins for vectorization;  you can write this 

     for (n in 1:N1){ 

         MU1[n] ~ normal(0,100); 
     }

You were totally right on all of these things! I also had to change the initial condition for the states, so that it draws from the unconditional distribution. 

Thank you!!

messages.author: fde4048c840328bf
messages.subject: Stochastic Volatility Models
parts:
Hi guys,

I am wondering how STAN deals with a non-linear model like a Stochastic Volatility (SV) one. I attach here a stan file that describes an AR(2) process with SV (and other exogenous regressors), where the error term of the regression is parametrized as in Kim, Sephard and Chib (1998), that is,

exp(h(t)/2)*e(t),e(t)~N(0,1)

The code compiles, and runs. However, I do not know if I am taking a too naive approach here and if the results that I am getting are not proper... SV models are tricky, and usually people (including myself) focus on the approximations derived in Kim et al's paper, or, more recently, using particle filters. Is there any reason why it should not work in STAN? If it works, I think this is a great improvement...

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Stochastic Volatility Models
parts:
I added the Kim, Shephard and Chib (1998) model
as an example. You can see the model(s) and the R
code to generate and test on simulated data in:

src/models/misc/moving-avg/

You can browse these on the web through GitHub:

https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/tree/master/src/models/misc/moving-avg

There is a straightforward implementation and a much
more efficient version with faster convergence (tens of samples versus
hundreds), better mixing, and faster iterations.

We need to reorganize our example models, so they probably
won't be on the above (slightly confusing) path forever.
I did add a section to the time-series chapter of the manual
describing the model, its conversion to Stan, and its
optimization.

Comments on these models or suggestions for other illustrative
models gladly accepted. I'm trying to keep the examples simple,
so I'm not mixing autoregression and stochastic volatility in
the model as Carlos did in the original post.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Stochastic Volatility Models (predictive simulation)
parts:
You can do it one of two ways.

1. Declare the values to simulate as parameters and
copy the bits of the model for them, or

2. Declare the values as generated quantities and
code up the data-generation model using _rng.

The latter is faster and usually generates better samples
(1 effective sampler per iteration), but it requires coding
the model twice.

- Bob
